newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian leaders hope to bury race row.
newsitem.headline: Australian leaders hope to bury race row.

text.p: Australian political and business leaders were hoping on Thursday that a parliamentary resolution condemning racism would help them turn the corner on a long and damaging row over immigration and race.
The resolution, adopted by both houses of parliament on Wednesday, reaffirmed Australia's commitment to equal rights, cultural diversity and a non-discriminatory immigration policy.

Opposition Labor Party leader Kim Beazley saw it as a "circuit breaker" to cut short an emotional debate that began on September 10 with a fiery anti-immigration speech by independent politician Pauline Hanson.
For Prime Minister John Howard, it was a "signal to the region that Australia is still in business as a decent society".
The conservative prime minister has been heavily criticised at home for his refusal to clearly condemn Hanson for warning that Australia was being "swamped by Asians".
But the criticism that appeared to hurt most came from Asian newspapers that accused Howard of condoning racist attitudes by his silence.
Wednesday's motion was widely interpreted as a damage-limitation exercise, and the first signs were that it might be working.
"In foreign affairs, what matters is the attitude and conduct of governments, not the statement made by one politician," Singapore Foreign Minister S. Jayakumar told reporters on a visit to Canberra.
"The bipartisan motion yesterday put this matter to rest," added Singapore High Commissioner Winston Choo.

Milton Hill, chief analyst of the Media Monitors organisation which has tracked media coverage of the row, said emotions could start to subside after parliament's gesture but immigration as an issue was not about to go away.
"I think it should help to bury it (the row) at a political level, but the issue and points raised will be with us for some time to come," Hill said.
Hill said the race debate had received almost unparalleled coverage in Australian media since Hanson made her maiden speech.

In the 50 days since her speech, the Queensland MP has drawn twice as much media attention as the economy and possible interest rate cuts and three times as much as Australia's traditional spring football grand finals.
But most surprising, said Hill, was the length of the debate: "Most issues come off the agenda within two or three weeks -- this one's going on and on."
If the row does finally subside, Australian business leaders will be especially relieved.

Officials of the Australian tourism industry, which brings in more than A$14 billion ($11 billion) in annual export earnings, told a conference in Perth on Thursday some groups of Asian tourists were already calling off Australian holidays.
"Nearly two million tourists come from Asia each year and this figure is set to grow dramatically over the next decade," said Bruce Baird, managing director of the Tourism Council of Australia.
"It is essential the tourism industry is not jeopardised by ill-informed comments on immigration," he added.
